vignette:
He is 53 now, a married man who has spent most of his adult life working as a social worker, the kind of person colleagues describe as steady, thoughtful, and easy to trust. When he first begins to speak about what happened, he does so in the same measured tone he uses when talking about difficult cases. But the story does not stay orderly for long. Certain details come out sharply, while others disappear behind long silences and a tightening in his jaw.

The assault happens in his late twenties, when he is still new to the profession and working hard to prove himself. He is assigned to community outreach and often meets clients in unpredictable settings, telling himself that flexibility and rapport are part of doing the job well. One evening, after what he believes is a routine meeting connected to a case, he is sexually assaulted by someone he had not understood to be a threat until it is already underway. What stays with him most is not only the physical violation, but the stunned disbelief that he cannot stop it, cannot think clearly, cannot make his body respond the way he expects. He remembers leaving in a daze, trying to act normal, focusing on practical things like getting home, washing his clothes, and making sure no one notices anything unusual.

In the days after, he tells no one. He feels overwhelmed by shame almost immediately, but it is mixed with something harder for him to admit: humiliation. He keeps returning to the thought that he should have known better, should have been stronger, should have read the situation sooner. As a man, and especially as someone trained to assess risk and protect vulnerable people, he cannot make sense of what happened without turning the blame onto himself. He goes back to work quickly and becomes even more reliable. He stays late, answers calls others ignore, and takes pride in being the person who can remain calm in a crisis. From the outside, he looks committed. Privately, he is trying not to feel anything at all.

He meets his future wife a few years later. He loves her and wants closeness with her, but intimacy is complicated from the start in ways he cannot explain. Sometimes he goes rigid when she touches him unexpectedly. Sometimes he dissociates during sex, drifting into a numb, faraway state while trying to act present. He learns to hide this by being attentive in other ways—cooking dinner, keeping track of schedules, fixing things around the house. When she asks if something is wrong, he says he is tired, stressed, preoccupied with work. Part of him believes that if he never names the assault, it will eventually lose its power.

Instead, his world grows smaller around it. He avoids certain neighborhoods, certain office buildings, certain kinds of meetings where he might be alone with a client or have to navigate unclear boundaries. He develops elaborate habits without quite admitting they are habits: sitting near exits, scanning rooms automatically, checking locks more than once before bed. He startles hard when someone comes up behind him. If he catches a particular cologne or hears a voice with a similar cadence to his assailant’s, his stomach drops and his thoughts scatter. On bad nights he wakes sweating from fragmented dreams he cannot fully describe, then lies beside his wife staring at the ceiling, listening for sounds in the house.

For years, he channels himself into work. As a social worker, he is skilled at helping others tell the truth about what has happened to them. He can sit with survivors of violence and speak gently about fear, coercion, and guilt. This is one of the bitter ironies of his life: he offers language to clients that he cannot use for himself. When male clients hint at sexual victimization, he feels his chest tighten. He remains composed in the room, but afterward he may lock himself in his office for a few minutes, breathing shallowly, hands trembling with an anger he cannot direct anywhere.

In his fifties, the strain becomes harder to contain. A case involving sexual abuse investigations stirs something loose, and around the same time his wife tells him she feels him disappearing even when he is sitting right beside her. He notices he is more irritable, snapping at small things, then feeling deeply ashamed. He is exhausted but cannot rest. Concentration, once one of his strengths, slips at work; he rereads reports without absorbing them. He avoids case discussions that touch too closely on assault, then berates himself for letting colleagues pick up the pieces. He feels detached from people he loves and yet constantly on guard around them, as if danger is always just outside his line of vision.

When he finally speaks about the assault aloud, he does not cry at first. He looks bewildered, as if he is describing something that happened to someone else. But underneath that distance is a grief he has carried for decades: grief for the younger man who walked home alone that night, for the years organized around secrecy, and for the life that has been shaped by fear in ways few people could see. Even now, in ordinary moments—hearing footsteps behind him in a hallway, staying late in an office with the door closed, feeling his wife reach for him in the dark—his body reacts before his mind can catch up, as though the past is not past at all.
